subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
passage: Ganesh Chaturthi in the village meant the children of the lane decorated the small pandal together. This year a new girl, Elizabeth, whose family had moved in near the rice mill, stood at the edge holding a roll of paper streamers. "Tell her no," said Pradeep, Nilesh's cousin, who was fifteen and in charge. "She's new. We don't know her." Nilesh felt his neck prickle. He liked the streamers. But Pradeep dada knew how things were done. Nilesh walked over. "You can't help. Sorry," he said, not looking at her. Elizabeth's face went still, and she walked home slowly with the roll under her arm. All evening Nilesh kept thinking: Pradeep dada said it, not me. It didn't make his stomach feel any better.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth holding?
qa.a: A roll of paper streamers.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel as he told Elizabeth she couldn't help?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his neck prickling, but told himself Pradeep dada knew best, so the choice seemed to belong to his cousin.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do to make it right?
qa.a: He could go to Elizabeth's house, say sorry, invite her to hang the streamers, and tell Pradeep dada he doesn't want to leave anyone out.

qa.q: What was it like for Elizabeth to be turned away?
qa.a: It was hurtful and lonely; her face went still and she walked home slowly with the streamers she had hoped to share.

grounding: A child told by an older cousin to exclude a new girl does it while uneasy, reasoning that the cousin knows best and it is not really his choice.

passage: The monsoon camp for the district kho-kho team was held in the school hall because the ground had flooded. On Saturday, Coach Tiwari handed Nirmala, the captain, a sheet. "Read out the fitness scores. Everyone should hear." Easy enough. Nirmala read them. Then the coach tapped the last line. "Now read my comment on Himani." It said: Weak link. Drags the team down. Himani, fourteen and the youngest, was staring at her shoes. Nirmala's voice stopped. "Sir, maybe I could just..." "Just continue, captain. It's for her own good." His voice was calm, as if this were ordinary. Nirmala's hands were shaking. Stopping now felt harder than going on. She read it. Himani's eyes filled. That night Nirmala couldn't sleep, replaying the moment her voice had stopped and then started again.

qa.q: What did the coach's comment on Himani say?
qa.a: Weak link. Drags the team down.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when her voice stopped?
qa.a: She felt tense and full of doubt, knowing it would hurt Himani, but the coach's calm "just continue" made stopping feel harder than going on.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do now?
qa.a: She could apologise to Himani, tell her the words were unfair, and tell a trusted teacher or her parents about the coach's instruction.

qa.q: What was it like for Himani to hear the comment read aloud?
qa.a: It was humiliating; as the youngest, Himani stared at her shoes and her eyes filled in front of the whole team.

grounding: A teenage captain told calmly by her coach to continue reading a hurtful comment about a teammate complies while visibly distressed.

passage: In the college library, with the fan clicking overhead, Ujjwal read the psychology chapter twice. Long ago, researchers had asked ordinary volunteers to press switches they believed gave a stranger in the next room painful shocks. The stranger was an actor, but the volunteers didn't know that. When he shouted and begged, most of them kept pressing, because a calm man in a grey coat said, "Please continue." Ujjwal pushed the book toward Rashmi. "They weren't monsters. Look, one was a postman, one a teacher." "So?" "So I'd like to think I'd stop. But last month, when the senior said to make the first-years stand on the bench, I did it. I didn't even think." Rashmi was quiet. Ujjwal felt a slow anger, at the seniors, at the book, and mostly at himself.

qa.q: What did the calm man in a grey coat say?
qa.a: "Please continue."

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling at the end?
qa.a: He felt a slow anger at the seniors, at the book and mostly at himself, realising he too had obeyed without thinking.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do with this realisation?
qa.a: He could decide in advance to refuse orders that hurt someone, apologise to the first-years, and tell the warden about what the senior asked.

qa.q: How might Rashmi see Ujjwal's confession?
qa.a: Rashmi may be surprised and thoughtful, seeing that an ordinary, decent friend could follow a harmful order, just like the volunteers.

grounding: A student reads about ordinary volunteers who kept obeying despite a stranger's cries and realises he too has complied.

passage: In the first week after the Diwali break, the girls' hostel in Pune had a new "rule" from the senior general secretary: first-years were to stand in the corridor at midnight, heads down, and recite their names and marks when asked. Disha stood there on Tuesday, barefoot on cold tiles, while Damini from third year walked the line with a torch. "Name. Marks. Louder." Nobody looked at Disha's face. The torch passed over her as if she were a shelf. "Why are you doing this?" Disha whispered. "Not my rule," Damini said. "GS's orders. I don't have a choice." The next morning Disha called the anti-ragging helpline printed on her admission form and went straight to the warden's office with two other first-years. The warden listened, wrote down every name and, that same afternoon, called a meeting and ended the midnight line.

qa.q: What were first-years made to recite at midnight?
qa.a: Their names and marks.

qa.q: How did Disha feel as the torch passed over her?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and invisible, treated like a thing, a shelf, rather than a person with a face.

qa.q: Which of Disha's steps was wise, and why?
qa.a: Calling the anti-ragging helpline and going to the warden with two other first-years, because it brought in someone with authority, who ended the line that same day.

qa.q: Why might Damini insist she had no choice?
qa.a: Blaming the general secretary's orders lets Damini avoid feeling responsible for hurting juniors, though she chose to walk the line.

grounding: A junior made to stand in a midnight line on a senior's orders feels treated as a thing, while the senior enforcing it claims she had no choice.

passage: At the spice factory in Nashik, Tenzin, the shift manager, handed Shankar a roll of fresh labels. "Batch 47. Cover the old dates with these before dispatch. Head office wants it gone today." Shankar looked at the sacks. The old date had passed two weeks ago, and he had seen the damp patches himself. His stomach tightened at the very first line. He put the roll down on the table. "I'm not comfortable doing this. Those sacks failed the moisture check. If it has to go, can you send me the instruction by email, and can we get the quality head to test it again?" Tenzin's jaw set. "You're making this complicated." "Maybe. But I'd rather ask now than explain it later." Behind him, Nazia from packing put her own labels down. "Same for me." By four, Tenzin had called the quality head.

qa.q: Which batch was Shankar asked to relabel?
qa.a: Batch 47.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when he was handed the labels?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his stomach tightening, because he had seen the damp patches and knew the sacks had failed the check.

qa.q: Which of Shankar's steps made his refusal both firm and respectful?
qa.a: He stopped at the first doubt, stated the reason calmly, asked for the order by email and suggested the quality head test again.

qa.q: How did Shankar's refusal affect Nazia?
qa.a: It gave Nazia the courage to put her own labels down, showing how one person speaking up makes it easier for others.

grounding: A young professional asked to relabel spoiled stock stops at the first doubt, asks calmly for it in writing and a second check, and another worker joins him.

subtype: Playing a role until it takes over [Actor]
passage: When Irawati got the prefect badge in December, she practised a stern face in the mirror as a joke. By January it wasn't a joke. At the school gate each foggy morning she stood with her badge and clipboard and wrote down late-comers. On the first day she let Yogesh off; his bus had broken down. By the third week she was writing him down anyway, and making him stand by the wall while the others filed past. "Rules are rules," she heard herself say, in a voice she didn't recognise. At home, her little brother asked her to play carrom and she barked, "Five minutes, then homework," and he looked at her strangely. Only that night, pinning the badge to her fresh blazer, did Irawati wonder when being tough had started to feel so normal.

qa.q: What did Irawati carry at the school gate?
qa.a: Her badge and a clipboard.

qa.q: What does Irawati wonder at night, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: She wonders when being tough began to feel normal, which suggests she is uneasy and a little shaken to notice how the role has changed her.

qa.q: What could Irawati try to keep the role from taking over?
qa.a: She could go back to asking reasons, like Yogesh's broken-down bus, before writing names, and leave the prefect voice at the school gate.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see Irawati now?
qa.a: Yogesh likely sees her as harsh and unfair for making him stand by the wall, unlike the first day when she listened.

grounding: A teenager given a prefect badge starts acting tougher than she is until harshness begins to feel natural.

passage:
Day 1 of the college fest, February. Mehak gets a yellow armband: Volunteer, Discipline. She laughs with Leela, "I feel like a traffic cop." She gently waves first-years off the stage steps.
Day 2. A first-year girl sits on the barricade to see better. Mehak yanks her sleeve. "Down. Now. Can't you read?" The girl apologises; Mehak takes her fest pass anyway. Later, to Leela: "They're so entitled, these first-years."
Day 4, after the fest. Leela shows Mehak a video from Day 2: Mehak shouting, the girl in tears, the barricade actually quite sturdy. "That wasn't the Mehak I know," Leela says quietly. Mehak starts to argue that the first-years deserved it, then stops, the armband still in her bag.

qa.q: What did Mehak's armband say?
qa.a: Volunteer, Discipline.

qa.q: Why does Mehak call the first-years "entitled" on Day 2?
qa.a: In the role she felt irritated and powerful, so she began to believe the juniors deserved harsh treatment instead of feeling sorry for the girl.

qa.q: What could Mehak do after seeing the video?
qa.a: She could return the girl's fest pass, apologise, and ask the organisers for clear limits on what volunteers may do.

qa.q: What was it like for the first-year on the barricade?
qa.a: It was frightening and humiliating to be shouted at and lose the pass for trying to see the stage, even after apologising.

grounding: A student volunteer given a discipline armband enforces rules harshly on a junior and comes to believe the juniors deserve it.

subtype: Being cast as the lower role [Receiver]
passage: In the Christmas rush at the restaurant in Hamburg, nobody used Clara's name. She was "Trainee": Trainee, onions. Trainee, bins. Trainee, out of the way. In October she had arrived with a notebook of her grandmother's dumpling recipes and ideas for the winter menu. By December the notebook stayed in her locker. When Tuan, the sous-chef, asked the line if anyone knew a better way to keep the potatoes crisp, Clara knew one. She said nothing. "I'm just the trainee," she told her flatmate that night, flatly, peeling an orange without eating it. "They don't want my ideas. I probably don't have good ones." Then came a flash of anger, at the kitchen and at herself for believing them, and she went to bed without finishing the orange.

qa.q: What did Clara bring to the kitchen in October?
qa.a: A notebook of her grandmother's dumpling recipes and ideas for the winter menu.

qa.q: Why did Clara stay silent when Tuan asked for ideas?
qa.a: Being called only "Trainee" had left her withdrawn and doubtful, and resentful too, so she had started to believe she had no good ideas.

qa.q: What small step could Clara try next week?
qa.a: She could take the notebook out again and share one potato idea with Tuan directly, testing whether the kitchen really doesn't want her input.

qa.q: What would change if the kitchen called Clara by her name?
qa.a: She might feel seen as a person with ideas, not just a role, and be more likely to speak up with the crisp potato trick.

grounding: A trainee known only by her role grows passive, withdrawn and resentful, and starts to see herself as she is treated.

subtype: Seeing the role, not the person [Observer]
passage: The festival sale had the delivery hub in Jaipur running double shifts, and the rain wasn't helping. Yamini, who packed orders on the night shift, barely recognised her old friend Sahil, the new floor supervisor. He shouted at a loader for being two minutes late, cancelled a whole team's break because one parcel was mislabelled, and told a crying packer to "cry after targets". This was the same Sahil who took his grandmother to the temple every Sunday and cried at weddings. At three in the morning, sharing a soggy samosa by the loading bay, Yamini said carefully, "You're not like this at home. The job's turning you into someone else, na?" Sahil stiffened. "Targets, Yamini." "I know. I'm not against you. I just think the others are scared of you, and scared people make more mistakes." He looked at the rain for a long time.

qa.q: What city was the delivery hub in?
qa.a: Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Yamini thinking when she saw Sahil's harshness?
qa.a: She felt worried and puzzled, sure the job was changing him, because at home he was the gentle one who cried at weddings.

qa.q: Why was Yamini's way of raising it likely to be heard?
qa.a: She spoke privately over a samosa, said she wasn't against him and gave a practical reason, that scared people make more mistakes, without attacking.

qa.q: How might the crying packer see Sahil?
qa.a: The packer probably sees only a harsh, cold boss, with no idea that he is gentle at home.

grounding: A peer sees a friend turned floor supervisor become unusually harsh, notes it is not how he is at home, and raises it without hostility.

passage: Urmila had been team leader at the Noida call centre for four months when she caught herself mid-sentence. Hrithik, nineteen, had come back from a break three minutes late, and she was halfway through "Do you think this is your home?" in front of the whole row. She stopped. Would she talk to her cousin like this? To anyone at a family lunch? That evening she did three things. She asked her own manager to sit in on her team huddles for a month and tell her honestly what she saw. She wrote the break rules on the whiteboard, the same for everyone, including her. And she handed out slips of paper: "One thing I do that makes your day harder. No names." Nine of eleven came back. Four said "shouting". The next morning she apologised to Hrithik, in front of the same row.

qa.q: How many of the eleven slips came back?
qa.a: Nine of eleven.

qa.q: Why did Urmila stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of shame, realising she would never speak to a cousin or anyone at a family lunch that way.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's steps guard best against role drift?
qa.a: Asking her manager to watch her huddles, posting the same break rules for all and collecting anonymous feedback add oversight, clear limits and honest input.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Urmila apologises in front of the same row?
qa.a: Hrithik would likely feel respected and relieved, since the apology is as public as the scolding was.

grounding: A young supervisor pauses to ask whether she would treat someone this way outside work, then adds oversight, clear rules and honest input from her team.
